title: A Aftermath for the Language
premise: After their mother's funeral, Isandro Okafor sorts through a house of unopened letters and unlabeled photographs, cataloging a silence that always defined her. Then a radio plays a song Isandro knows was never recorded — a song written in a notebook they just inherited — and the trail leads to a stranger, Adaora, who claims to have co-written it and to have been erased from every photograph and every story. As Isandro investigates, they uncover evidence their mother committed a quiet, lifelong theft: of songs, credit, and a friendship. The novel ends with Isandro publicly restoring Adaora's name at a small memorial concert, choosing truth over loyalty to the dead, and finally learning to smile in a way that begins conversations instead of ending them.
about_author: Felix Coldharbour is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging other people's unfinished manuscripts before writing his own. He lives near a defunct record press and writes about inheritance, music, and the debts families never settle.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: Isandro Okafor, POV. A week after the funeral, Isandro methodically catalogs their mother's belongings — sealed letters, unlabeled photographs, an untouched piano. Their practiced smile deflects every condolence. Emotional beat: grief managed as bureaucracy, control mistaken for closure.

chapters.title: A Song on the Radio
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. Driving home from the estate lawyer's office, Isandro hears a song on a late-night community station and recognizes it word for word from a notebook in their mother's desk — a song she wrote and, supposedly, never recorded or shared. Emotional beat: the first crack in the curated past.

chapters.title: The Notebook Problem
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. At home, Isandro compares the notebook to a recording of the broadcast; the lyrics match exactly, including a verse crossed out. They begin pulling photographs from boxes and notice one figure repeatedly cropped or cut away. Emotional beat: unease sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. In a 1980s photo from a Lagos recording studio, Isandro finds the excised woman half-visible at the frame's edge. On the back, in their mother's hand: 'Adaora — do not contact.' Emotional beat: the inheritance curdles into a question.

chapters.title: Adaora
chapters.summary: Adaora Eze, POV. Now in her seventies, teaching music to children in a decaying community hall, Adaora receives Isandro's careful letter and burns it without reading past the name Okafor. Emotional beat: forty years of justified anger, worn smooth but not gone.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Remember
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. Isandro interviews aging musicians from their mother's circle, collecting contradictory hagiographies. One drunk trumpeter lets slip that 'your mother didn't write everything she signed.' Emotional beat: loyalty beginning to feel like complicity.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. Among the sealed correspondence, Isandro finds one letter addressed to them, dated years ago, never sent: their mother admitting there was 'a debt I could not pay in money.' It names no one. Emotional beat: the parent's silence reinterpreted as cowardice.

chapters.title: Community Hall, Thursday Evenings
chapters.summary: Adaora, POV. Isandro shows up at Adaora's class; she refuses to speak, but lets them stay and watch. A child mangles a chord and Adaora corrects it with tenderness Isandro has never seen directed at them. Emotional beat: recognition across a wall of grievance.

chapters.title: Versions of 1987
chapters.summary: Alternating recollections, framed by Isandro's notes. Adaora and the mother were collaborators until a contract, a pregnancy, and a betrayal separated them; each woman's version assigns blame differently. Emotional beat: truth revealed as contested territory, not buried treasure.

chapters.title: The Contract
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. In the lawyer's files Isandro finds the original publishing agreement — their mother's sole signature where two names should be, notarized by a man now dying in a care home. Emotional beat: justice stops being abstract and acquires paperwork.

chapters.title: The Notary's Confession
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. The dying notary tells Isandro he witnessed the removal of Adaora's name under pressure from the label, and that their mother paid him for silence for decades. He asks if forgiveness can be arranged posthumously. Emotional beat: horror tempered by pity.

chapters.title: Loyalty, Audited
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. Isandro's brother Chidi arrives, furious that Isandro is 'airing' their mother's secrets, threatening to contest the estate. Family dinner collapses. Emotional beat: Isandro realizes loyalty to the dead may be its own kind of theft.

chapters.title: The Unrecorded Verse
chapters.summary: Adaora, POV. Adaora finally opens up: the crossed-out verse was written for her stillborn daughter, and hearing it on the radio — credited solely to the mother — reopened the grave. She gives Isandro her half of the notebook pages. Emotional beat: grief meeting grief as equals.

chapters.title: Time Already Running Out
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. The label announces a remastered anniversary edition of the mother's catalog, cementing the false credits permanently. Isandro has weeks, not years, to act. Emotional beat: urgency replacing mourning; the clock becomes a character.

chapters.title: Chidi's Bargain
chapters.summary: Chidi, POV. Chidi offers Isandro a deal: bury the evidence, split the royalties quietly, protect the family name. Isandro sees in Chidi their own old smile, perfected. Emotional beat: temptation made flesh, refused with difficulty.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. Isandro breaks into the label's archive (with a sympathetic retired engineer's help) and finds session tapes proving Adaora sang lead on demos never released. They copy everything. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, hands shaking, certain anyway.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Piano
chapters.summary: Adaora and Isandro, alternating. Isandro brings the tapes to Adaora; she plays the mother's upright piano for the first time in forty years and plays the stolen song whole, including the verse for her daughter. Neither apologizes yet; both understand. Emotional beat: catharsis before resolution.

chapters.title: The Cease-and-Desist
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. The label's lawyers threaten Isandro with ruin; Chidi sides with them publicly. Isandro loses friends, standing, and the estate's liquidity — and keeps going. Emotional beat: the cost of truth itemized and accepted.

chapters.title: Memorial Concert
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, mostly Isandro's POV. At a small hall, Isandro stages a memorial concert and, mid-program, publicly presents the tapes and restores Adaora's authorship before playing the song together. Adaora sings the unrecorded verse. Emotional beat: climax — public truth, private reconciliation beginning.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Adaora, POV. Legal fallout spreads; the label settles rather than litigate. Adaora is credited, interviewed, briefly famous, and finds it hollow except for one thing: strangers singing her daughter's verse back to her. Emotional beat: vindication that heals only partially.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV. Isandro visits the grave with the restored album and reads aloud the unsent letter's missing final page, found taped inside the piano bench — their mother's apology, written and hidden, too proud to send. Isandro forgives the stranger in the photographs, who was also their mother. Emotional beat: grief finally allowed to be love.

chapters.title: The Smile That Begins Conversations
chapters.summary: Isandro, POV, coda. Months later, Isandro teaches a Saturday songwriting class in Adaora's community hall. A student asks about the famous song; Isandro smiles — a new smile — and says, 'Let me tell you about two women and a notebook.' Emotional beat: inheritance transformed from debt into gift.
